pages.title: Where will a reaction begin?

blocks.text: An organic molecule can contain electron-rich and electron-poor regions even when its total charge is zero. A reagent often reacts at one particular atom rather than anywhere on the skeleton. Following electron density helps us predict this first encounter.

Electron-pair donation and acceptance provide a useful language for polar reactions. We then distinguish three ideas: local bond polarity, its transmission through σ bonds, and delocalisation through adjacent p orbitals. These describe different ways in which structure controls reactivity.

pages.transition: Begin with the species that can supply an electron pair.

pages.title: Electron-pair donors: nucleophiles

blocks.text: A nucleophile is a species that donates an electron pair to form a new bond. HO⁻ and CN⁻ have available electron pairs; neutral H2O and NH3 can also act as nucleophiles because oxygen and nitrogen possess lone pairs.

When NH3 bonds to an electron-deficient carbon, nitrogen supplies its lone pair. Its lack of an initial negative charge does not prevent donation. Decide whether a pair is available and where it can be donated, rather than defining every nucleophile simply as a negative ion.
Electronegativity measures an atom’s attraction for shared electrons. A lone pair is a pair not used in an ordinary bond; electron deficiency means a centre can benefit from accepting a pair.

pages.transition: The partner must provide a place that can accept that pair.

pages.title: Electron-pair acceptors: electrophiles

blocks.text: An electrophile accepts an electron pair in forming a bond. CH3⁺ is electron deficient. An uncharged molecule may also have an electrophilic centre: in CH3I, the polar C–I bond leaves carbon partially positive; in a carbonyl group, oxygen withdraws electron density from carbon.

In CH3I + HO⁻ → CH3OH + I⁻, the hydroxide oxygen donates a lone pair to carbon, while the C–I bond pair moves to iodine. Both arrows are necessary to preserve carbon’s allowed bonding: a new bond does not simply accumulate alongside all its original bonds.

pages.transition: Curved arrows let us record both donation and bond breaking.

pages.title: Curved arrows follow actual electrons

blocks.text: Start a full curved arrow at the electron source: a lone pair or a bond. End it where the pair is used, at an atom or in a new bond region. A full arrow follows two electrons; a fish-hook arrow follows one in a radical process.

The arrow does not start at a positive charge or show an atom flying across the page. In a bond-breaking arrow, start at the bond being broken and point towards the atom receiving its pair. Check charges before and after the step as well as the atom counts.

pages.transition: Before a reagent arrives, polar bonds can already create unequal electron density.

pages.title: Induction: a pull along sigma bonds

blocks.text: The inductive effect is permanent polarisation of σ bonds caused by electronegativity differences. In CH3CH2Cl, chlorine attracts the C–Cl pair, leaving Cl δ− and the adjacent carbon δ+. This polarisation influences neighbouring bonds, with an effect that decreases rapidly with distance.

Partial charges, δ+ and δ−, describe unequal sharing; they are smaller than full ionic charges. Electrons have not simply transferred completely to chlorine in chloroethane. A permanent effect means it exists without an attacking reagent, not that the molecule can never react.

pages.transition: The direction of that permanent influence gives the +I and −I labels.

pages.title: Donating and withdrawing groups

blocks.text: Relative to hydrogen, electron-withdrawing groups show a −I effect and electron-donating groups a +I effect. Halogens, –NO2 and –CN withdraw inductively; alkyl groups commonly donate. The sign identifies the direction of influence on the attached carbon framework.

Chlorine near a carboxyl group helps stabilise the negative charge of the carboxylate formed after H⁺ is lost. This explains why chloroacetic acid is stronger than acetic acid. Moving chlorine farther away weakens its inductive influence; the number and position of substituents both matter.

pages.transition: Some electronic distributions need more than local σ-bond polarisation to describe them.

pages.title: One drawing may not describe the electrons

blocks.text: Resonance is needed when one Lewis structure cannot adequately represent a species. Contributing structures keep the same positions and connections of nuclei but change the placement of electrons. The real species is a resonance hybrid, with electrons delocalised across the relevant orbitals.

Benzene’s two familiar alternating-bond drawings do not represent molecules switching back and forth. Its actual carbon framework has equivalent C–C bonds and delocalised π electrons. The hybrid is more stable than an individual localised contributor; resonance is a model of that one structure.

pages.transition: We should compare valid contributors without mistaking them for separate substances.

pages.title: Which contributors matter more?

blocks.text: Contributors with complete octets, more covalent bonds and less unnecessary charge separation generally contribute more. If charges occur, a negative charge is better accommodated on a more electronegative atom. These are guides for comparing drawings of the same species.

For a carbonyl group, a neutral C=O contributor and a charge-separated C+–O− contributor help explain its polarisation. They have identical atom connections. The charge-separated contributor does not mean the sample contains a separate bottle of carbocation–oxide molecules.

pages.transition: Connected p orbitals also let substituents donate or withdraw by resonance.

pages.title: Resonance donation and withdrawal

blocks.text: A +R effect donates electron density from a substituent into a conjugated system; lone-pair groups such as –OH or –NH2 can do this when correctly connected. A −R effect withdraws electron density through conjugation; –NO2 and –CN are common examples.

Conjugation requires adjacent orbitals capable of overlap; resonance is not transmitted unchanged through an arbitrary saturated chain. A group may withdraw by induction yet donate by resonance. State the effect and the bonding environment rather than labelling a group universally “donating”.

Compare the same –OH group attached directly to a conjugated ring with one separated from it by a saturated CH2. Its lone pair cannot be conjugated directly into the ring through that intervening sp3 carbon. Always inspect the actual orbital connections before claiming resonance donation.

pages.transition: The donor, acceptor and bonding network now tell us which explanation to use.

blocks.text: Identify the donor pair and the accepting centre before drawing arrows. Nucleophile/electrophile labels describe a reaction role; either partner may be neutral or charged. Full arrows move pairs, and fish-hook arrows move single electrons.

Induction polarises σ bonds and fades with distance. Resonance delocalises electrons through connected orbitals without moving nuclei. Use correct contributors to explain where electron density lies; never interpret them as separate isomers or rapidly interconverting structures.

questions.question: Can water be a nucleophile despite having no charge?
questions.answer: Yes. Oxygen has lone pairs that can be donated to an electron-pair acceptor.

questions.question: Where do the two curved arrows start in hydroxide substitution on CH3I?
questions.answer: One starts at an oxygen lone pair and ends at carbon; the other starts at the C–I bond and ends at iodine.

questions.question: Why does a chlorine substituent have a weaker acid-strength effect farther from –COOH?
questions.answer: Its inductive withdrawal is transmitted through σ bonds and decreases rapidly with distance.

questions.question: Do nuclei move between resonance contributors?
questions.answer: No. Their positions and connectivity remain fixed; only electron placement changes.

questions.question: Can –OH show both electron withdrawal and donation?
questions.answer: Yes. It withdraws inductively through a σ bond and can donate a lone pair by resonance when conjugated with the attached system.
